extracted.intended_audience: policy professionals, health-care policy scholars, journalists, and interested members of the public following administrative/state health-care regulation
extracted.subtask_description: An opinion/analysis of how the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) has accumulated regulatory power and the implications for the division of labor between Congress and the agency in U.S. health care policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original congressional intent: limited federal role
rubrics_metrics.description: When Congress approved the original legislation creating Medicare and Medicaid, the intention was for the federal government to play a carefully circumscribed role in the evolution of American health care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a baseline normative standard: evaluate contemporary policy and agency actions against the historical expectation that federal involvement should be limited and narrowly defined. The piece uses this as a contrast to later expansions of agency power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegation of rulemaking based on broad guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress regularly tasked CMS ... with writing specific rules for establishing new terms for payments based on broad guidance (such as using cost reports from a certain year to build 'prospective payments' going forward, with adjustments for politically sensitive factors such as local labor costs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat broad statutory delegations that permit detailed, technical rulemaking by CMS as a criterion for agency-driven policy evolution. Note that such delegations often lead to extensive administrative rulemaking rather than legislative action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of open-ended authorities to set standards
rubrics_metrics.description: As these powers were handed over to CMS, they often came with additional open-ended authorities to establish quality standards, ensure fair access for underserved populations, police fraud and abuse, and much else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether statutory delegations grant 'open-ended' authority enabling agencies to expand into domains that may exceed Congress's original intent; consider the range of authorities (quality, access, fraud policing) as markers of scope expansion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of the ACA on agency authority (breadth of delegation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Affordable Care Act (ACA) in 2010 famously included nearly 3,000 references to the secretary of the Department of Health and Human Service — mostly as part of new delegations of regulatory powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the number and scope of statutory cross-references/delegations (e.g., to the HHS secretary) as an indicator of how much regulatory discretion Congress conferred; examine concrete examples (minimum benefit standards, marketplace rules, accounting guidelines) to assess practical impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency rulemaking can create substantive requirements absent new Congressional action
rubrics_metrics.description: This year, CMS published a 284-page final rule, without any prompting from Congress, outlining new requirements for insurers sponsoring Medicaid managed care plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether major substantive regulatory changes originate from agency initiative rather than legislative direction; consider scale (page count, scope) and whether the rule imposes material obligations on regulated parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of operational compliance tools (e.g., 'secret shoppers')
rubrics_metrics.description: Among the many new requirements in the published regulation is a mandate for states to deploy 'secret shoppers' to test insurers’ compliance with new access-to-care standards, including wait times for primary care appointments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess appropriateness and intrusiveness of compliance testing mechanisms agencies require of states/insurers; consider evidence base, administrative burden, and implications for provider/insurer behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation imposing input-cost floors without payment adjustments (unfunded mandates)
rubrics_metrics.description: CMS moved forward with minimum staffing requirements for nursing homes that are receiving payments from Medicare and Medicaid. The new floor on input costs for these institutions was not tied to higher payments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat regulations that mandate higher inputs (staffing, equipment, etc.) without corresponding funding as problematic; evaluate fiscal impact on providers and potential unintended consequences when new standards are unfunded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual comprehensive rules (Medicare Advantage example) as a vehicle for major policy changes
rubrics_metrics.description: CMS’s 2024 Medicare Advantage rule (a new one is issued annually) runs over 400 pages in the Federal Register. Among this year’s new requirements are restrictions on compensation arrangements with insurance brokers, new access to care tests for various covered services, and formula adjustments limiting pay bumps for patient risk factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the scale and frequency of agency rulemaking (e.g., annual omnibus rules) as a criterion for assessing how agencies effect recurring, substantive policy shifts; examine specific provisions for market impacts (broker compensation, access tests, risk-adjustment formulas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Waiver negotiation process dominated by agency rulebook with limited congressional/public oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Within Medicaid, states can petition the federal government for 'waivers' of certain statutory requirements ... Much of the Medicaid program is now governed by federal-state waiver negotiations that occur without significant public oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the transparency and accountability of waiver processes: whether statutory constraints are sufficient, whether CMS-drafted 'rulebook' terms substitute for clear legislative standards, and whether public oversight is adequate during negotiation and implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferred policy posture: Congress sets clear market rules with less ongoing intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: If the intention is for the federal government to essentially run US health care, Congress will never be able to occupy the driver’s seat. ... The outlook might be different if Congress stepped back from trying to run the health system and instead set clear market rules governing transactions between suppliers of insurance, medical services providers, and consumers, with less ongoing governmental interference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the degree to which Congress sets durable, clear market rules (as opposed to continuous delegated micromanagement) as a positive standard; assess proposals by how well they create stable, rule-based market governance rather than ongoing agency discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political reality constraint: congressional propensity to guarantee results
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the likelihood that political pressures will always push Congress toward trying to guarantee results in health care ... it is far more likely that, even with less judicial forbearance, CMS or an agency like it will continue to call most of the shots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating reform proposals, factor in political incentives: whether Congress will realistically resist interventionist responses to constituency pressures, and therefore whether changes will shift power away from agencies in practice.
